subject: maths
title: Chapter 8 · Test 4
summary: Chapter 8 test 4: 15 questions on probability, Venn diagrams, two-way tables, conditional and independent events, tree diagrams and counting.
body: This test covers all of Chapter 8: probability review, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, conditional probability, independent events, tree diagrams with and without replacement, and counting techniques. It has 15 multiple-choice questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes, no notes, no calculator unless the question says. Draw a quick tree, table or set of boxes on scrap paper when it helps, and check that every probability you find is between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: A bag holds 5 yellow, 11 purple and 9 orange marbles. One is taken at random. What is the probability that it is NOT orange?
questions.explanation: There are 25 marbles and 16 are not orange, so P = 16/25 = 16/25.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 9/25 is the probability that it IS orange. Use the complement.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you counted colours (2 of 3 colours). Count the items, not the colours.
mistakes.C: Step 3: you divided by the 9 orange marbles. A probability is out of the total, 25.

questions.prompt: The Venn diagram shows 24 people and whether they chose Art and/or Music. One person is picked at random. Find P(Art ∪ Music).
questions.explanation: Art ∪ Music is everything inside the circles: 6 + 2 + 9 = 17, so P = 17/24.
steps: ∪ means "or": every region inside either circle.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 2 is the overlap, Art ∩ Music. ∪ means everything inside either circle.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you left out the overlap. People in both circles are in the union too.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 8 is the whole Art circle. Add the "Music only" region as well.

questions.diagram_alt: A Venn diagram with ξ = 24: Art only 6, both 2, Music only 9, and 7 outside both circles

questions.prompt: Two printers work independently. P(printer A works) = 0.95 and P(printer B works) = 0.8. Find the probability that both work.
questions.explanation: The events are independent, so multiply: 0.95 × 0.8 = 0.76. Adding the probabilities is the common slip.
steps: The two events don't affect each other: independent.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added the probabilities. For "and" with independent events, multiply — a probability can't be more than 1.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is only the first event. Both must happen, so multiply by the second probability.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is only the second event. Both must happen, so multiply by the first probability.

questions.prompt: A new phone is ordered by choosing a colour (6 options), a storage size (3 options) and a case (2 options), as shown by the boxes. How many different orders are possible?
questions.explanation: Multiplication principle: 6 × 3 × 2 = 36. Adding gives far too few.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added the choices. Each choice goes with every other choice — multiply.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you forgot the third choice (Case). Multiply all three boxes.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you added the case choices at the end. Every box multiplies.

questions.diagram_alt: Three boxes marked ? for the number of choices, labelled Colour, Storage and Case, with multiplication signs between them

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the numbers added; the diagram shows every sum. What is the probability that the sum is 9?
questions.explanation: 4 of the 36 equally likely cells fit (3+6, 4+5, 5+4, 6+3), so P = 4/36 = 1/9. The 11 sums are not equally likely.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you counted each pair once (e.g. only one of 1 + 5 and 5 + 1). Every cell is a different outcome — count all 4.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the 11 sums are not equally likely. Use the 36 cells.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you put 4 cells over 11 sums. The total is the 36 equally likely cells.

questions.diagram_alt: A 6 by 6 grid with dice values 1 to 6 along the top and side; each cell shows the sum of the two values

questions.prompt: The two-way table has some blank cells. Complete it, then find the probability that a randomly chosen person from all 100 is in the "Year 8" row and the "No phone" column (marked ?).
steps: Divide by the grand total: P = 12/100 = 3/25.

mistakes.B: Step 3: you divided by the Year 8 row total. The person is chosen from all 100.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 28 is the Year 8 / Phone cell. Go on to the No phone column.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 50 is the whole No phone column. You need the Year 8 row only.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Phone, No phone, Total and rows Year 7, Year 8, Total. Year 7: Phone 22, Total 60. Year 8: No phone marked ?, Total 40. Total row: Phone 50, grand total 100. Other cells blank

questions.prompt: Use the two-way table. A person in the "Not" row is chosen at random. What is the probability that they are in the "Flu" column?
questions.explanation: Given Not, use only that row: 12 of its 80 are Flu, so P = 3/20. Dividing by the grand total ignores the condition.
steps: Given "Not": use only that row, 80 people.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you divided by all 200. Given "Not", divide by that row's total.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you divided by the Flu column — that is P(Not | Flu). The given group is the Not row.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 18/200 ignores the condition. Use only the Not row.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Flu, No flu, Total and rows Vaccinated (6, 114, 120), Not (12, 68, 80) and Total (18, 182, 200)

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: A pack has 8 working and 4 faulty light bulbs. Two bulbs are taken without replacement. Find the probability that both are faulty.
questions.explanation: Without replacement: 4/12 × 3/11 = 1/11. Using 4/12 twice forgets that the first one is not put back.
steps: Second pick: 11 left, 3 of the right type: 3/11.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 4/12 again is WITH replacement. One has gone, so use 3/11.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you changed the top but not the bottom. Only 11 are left.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you added the branches. Along a path, multiply.

questions.prompt: The 8 letters of TRIANGLE are arranged in a row so that the arrangement starts with T. How many arrangements are possible?
questions.explanation: Fix the restricted item (1 way), then arrange the other 7: 7! = 5040. 8! ignores the rule.
steps: Fill the restricted position first: 1 way.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 8! counts every order. The fixed item has only 1 place.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you subtracted from the total, which counts the orders that break the rule.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 7 items are left, but they can be arranged in many orders — use a factorial.

questions.prompt: Of 80 readers, 45 read fiction, 38 read non-fiction and 9 read neither. A reader is chosen at random. What is the probability that they read both?
questions.explanation: 80 − 9 = 71 are in at least one group, but 45 + 38 = 83, so 83 − 71 = 12 are counted twice: they are in both. P = 3/20.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 9 is the number in neither group. Use it to find the overlap.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 71/80 is P(at least one). "Both" is only the overlap.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 45 + 38 counts the "both" people twice — compare it with 71.

questions.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.8 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.9. Find P(A | B).
steps: Addition rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.4.

mistakes.A: Step 3: dividing by P(A) gives P(B | A). The given event is B.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is P(A ∩ B). Divide it by P(B).
mistakes.D: Step 3: you divided by P(A ∪ B). Divide by the given event, P(B).

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: At the first traffic light P(green) = 0.6. If it is green, P(second light green) = 0.9; if it is red, P(second light green) = 0.3 (see the tree diagram). Find the probability that exactly one of the two lights is green.
steps: Exactly one happens on two paths: Green then Red, or Red then Green.

mistakes.A: Step 3: that is only one path. The other order also gives exactly one — add both paths.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that path has two successes. You need exactly one.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 1 − P(none) is "at least one", which includes two successes.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Green 0.6 and Red 0.4; after Green, Green 0.9 and Red 0.1; after Red, Green 0.3 and Red 0.7

questions.prompt: A hospital has 2 backup generators. Each starts with probability 0.9, independently. Find the probability that at least one starts.

mistakes.A: Step 2: that is the chance they ALL succeed. "At least one" is 1 − P(none).
mistakes.B: Step 3: that is P(none). Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you added the probabilities. Use 1 − P(none) for "at least one".

questions.prompt: P(windy day) = 0.4. On a windy day the ferry is delayed with probability 0.5; on a calm day, with probability 0.1 (see the tree diagram). The ferry is delayed. What is the probability that it was windy?
questions.explanation: P(Delayed) = 0.4 × 0.5 + 0.6 × 0.1 = 0.26. P(Windy and Delayed) = 0.2. So P(Windy | Delayed) = 0.2 ÷ 0.26 = 10/13.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 0.5 is P(Delayed | Windy), the condition the wrong way round. Here Delayed is given.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 0.2 is P(Windy and Delayed). Divide it by P(Delayed).
mistakes.D: Step 3: that is P(Calm | Delayed), the other branch. Use the Windy path on top.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Windy 0.4 and Calm 0.6; after Windy, Delayed 0.5 and On time 0.5; after Calm, Delayed 0.1 and On time 0.9

questions.prompt: Two students are picked at random from a class of 12 to represent it. What is the probability that Noah and Isla are the two picked?
questions.explanation: Number of possible pairs = 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66, and only one of them is the pair wanted, so P = 1/66.
steps: Each pair is counted twice (in two orders), so there are 132 ÷ 2 = 66 pairs.
Only one pair is the one wanted: P = 1/66.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 12 × 11 counts ordered picks, but the pair can be picked in 2 orders. Divide by 2 first.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 2/12 is the chance that ONE particular person is chosen. Both must be chosen.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 12 × 12 lets the same person be picked twice. Count pairs of different people.
